description:
I'm a BS IT student and web developer interested in technology, innovation, space science, and problem-solving. I enjoy building useful digital projects and interactive experiences.

I'm looking for creative, motivated teammates skilled in programming, design, research, science, or communication. Teamwork, fresh ideas, and willingness to learn matter most.

Our current project is Lunar Quest, but we're open to exploring new ideas and building meaningful projects together.
summary: Lunar Quest is a free browser game for ages 7 to 12 that shows how hard it is to run a Moon base. Players have 14 days and a small daily power budget to split between air, radiation shielding, science and, in Explorer mode, a greenhouse. Every choice costs something: power spent on science is not spent on air or shielding. Real NASA space weather data decides how stormy each mission is, so a quiet week and a stormy week play differently. Players pick between two landing sites, a sunlit ridge and an icy crater floor, and learn from an end-of-mission debrief. It answers the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real mission trade-offs into a game kids can play in minutes, with no install and no account.
details: Lunar Quest is a single-page browser game built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript and hosted on GitHub Pages. Each day the player gets power and splits it between Air, Shield (piling moon dirt to block radiation), Science and, in Explorer mode, a Greenhouse. The crew breathes 3 air a day and eats 2 food a day, and a battery stores unused power. A mission is won by collecting 35 science points in 14 days. It ends early if the air or food runs out or the radiation dose reaches 36. Players choose between two landing sites. Sunlit Ridge has 10 power a day. Icy Crater Floor has 6 power a day but makes air, food and science more efficiently from water ice and has 10% less radiation. Real NASA DONKI solar flare data sets storm strength, and a 7-day check of flares, CMEs, Kp index and particle events decides how many storms a run has. A flare gives a one-day warning, and a storm shelter cuts extra radiation by 70% at the cost of that day's science. A real ISS radiation reading from NASA OSDR RadLab and a Moon-versus-Earth radiation comparison appear on the start and end screens, with links to learning resources from the Canadian Space Agency. The intended impact is that children learn that space missions are about trade-offs, and that space weather is a real danger astronauts plan for. The game states what is live and what is archived, falls back to a small set of real flares if NASA data is unavailable, and says plainly which numbers are simplified game values.
